clue.text: Ready to get engaged?

parts.note: engaged reads like betrothal, but here it means joining battle: someone in prime condition and eager for a scrap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Engaged' points to a wedding ring; the military sense of engaging the enemy is the one meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a boxer or soldier in peak condition, prepared for combat.

clue.text: Slack return in fielding

indicators.note: return asks for the run of letters to be read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the word fielding

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder is lazy about throwing the ball back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' picks ELDI out of fiELDIng and 'return' turns it round. Fielding and returns are cricket terms, but the cricket picture is only a cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Slack and idle both describe someone not working or a period of little activity.

clue.text: Army takes a long time to get a prisoner

parts.note: a host is an archaic word for an army or great multitude
an age is a very long time, as in 'it took ages'

explanation.surface: Troops spend ages capturing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A person held captive to force demands is a kind of prisoner.

clue.text: In a way, it means this month

parts.note: taken as written
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A remark about how a word is used to refer to the current month.
explanation.walkthrough: Business letters once wrote 'the 5th inst.' for the 5th of this month; the abbreviation of Latin instante is now old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation in old commercial correspondence denotes the current calendar month.

clue.text: His work is often framed

parts.note: framed suggests a picture or a criminal set-up, but it means fitted into window frames

explanation.walkthrough: 'Framed' tempts towards an artist or a stitched-up suspect; the worker meant fits panes of glass into frames.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who cuts and fits glass sets most of it into window or picture frames.

clue.text: I'd look up to one who's worshipped

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone admires a revered figure.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a figure or person venerated, sometimes excessively, like a god.

clue.text: Information in a scriptural form

indicators.note: form as a verb means to shape into a new arrangement, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Facts presented in the style of holy writ.
explanation.definitionFit: Particulars are the details or facts about something, as on a form asking for your personal details.

clue.text: When it's too humid to hunt?

definitions.text: When it's too humid to hunt?

parts.words: When it's too humid to hunt?
parts.note: humid is a synonym for close weather, and a period when hunting is banned has the same name

explanation.walkthrough: Close means muggy as well as shut; the joke treats the hunting ban as a weather report.
explanation.definitionFit: The period of the year when killing game or fish is prohibited is named this way.

clue.text: Course manual

parts.note: course suggests a study course, but it is a course of a meal, and the manual tells you how to make it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' looks like a training course's handbook; it is a dish served at dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of recipes is a guide to preparing the courses of a meal.

clue.text: Her charges are always small

parts.note: charges suggests fees, but it means the children in someone's care

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' sounds like a cheap tradesperson's bill; it means the little children a nanny looks after.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed to look after young children has only little ones in her care.

clue.text: In which to find an artist's early work?

definitions.text: In which to find an artist's early work?

parts.words: In which to find an artist's early work?
parts.note: early work hints at a painter's juvenilia, but means the rough first drafts drawn before a finished picture

explanation.walkthrough: Preliminary sketches are an artist's first work on a subject, kept in pads of drawing paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Pads for rough drawing hold the preliminary studies an artist makes before a finished work.

clue.text: It's bitter beer with nothing in it

indicators.note: in places the zero inside the drink

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
O is the letter shaped like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A complaint that a pint tastes harsh because it has no body.
explanation.definitionFit: The juice of this succulent plant has a notoriously bitter taste, used medicinally.

clue.text: Chance being called a lady?

explanation.surface: Someone speculates that fortune is personified as a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition recalls the phrase 'Lady Luck' and the song 'Luck Be a Lady'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune or chance is often personified as a woman, Lady Luck.

clue.text: Returns from business

parts.note: returns could be going home from work or tax forms, but means money received by a shop

explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' suggests a commuter coming home or goods sent back; here it means income.
explanation.definitionFit: The money a shop or business receives from sales is its receipts or income.

clue.text: Turns up for the bargains

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: spins are turns, rotations

explanation.surface: Someone appears at the sales looking for cheap deals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SPINS into the answer. Snips is informal British for bargains: 'it's a snip at that price'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snip is British slang for something remarkably cheap, a good deal.

clue.text: Put down an initial payment

explanation.surface: Someone hands over money up front.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something down is to place it, and a sum paid first to secure a purchase has the same name.

clue.text: Cord I twisted into a sort of column

indicators.note: twisted means the letters are wrung into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone winds rope around a pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: The plainest of the classical Greek architectural orders gives its name to a style of column.

clue.text: Witch's last choice of abode?

parts.note: an end is the last part of something
or is the word that offers a choice between options

explanation.surface: Wondering where a witch finally decided to live.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible (1 Samuel 28) King Saul consults the Witch of Endor, so her home is the answer, and the whole clue also gives the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament medium consulted by Saul is known by the town she lived in.

clue.text: Grain of discomfort

explanation.surface: A tiny bit of unease.
explanation.walkthrough: A corn is a hard patch of skin on a foot that causes pain; 'of' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheat or maize is cereal grain, and a painful callus on a toe is a common source of foot pain.

clue.text: Chief part of a bridge

explanation.surface: The main structural element of a span.
explanation.definitionFit: As a prefix it means principal, as in archenemy, and the curved support of a span is a structural element.

clue.text: Garden pest took shelter behind a piano

indicators.note: behind places the sheltering word after the two letters before it

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
hid means took shelter or concealed oneself

explanation.surface: A bug hid behind a piano in someone's garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenfly and blackfly are sap-sucking insects that damage roses and vegetables.

clue.text: It's meant to be read, so make it clear

indicators.note: make here means fashion or form the letters into something new

explanation.surface: Writing is for reading, so it should be lucid.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece in a newspaper or magazine is written for people to read.

clue.text: Academic accepts phil, perhaps, as school member

indicators.note: accepts means one word takes another inside it

parts.note: a don is a university teacher

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters may be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A professor admits a student named Phil to a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' suggests a pupil, but the member is of a school of sea creatures; Phil is just a name, so the anagram signal 'perhaps' hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: These marine mammals swim in groups called pods or schools.

clue.text: A sailor scowls about Herculean tasks

indicators.note: about means the word wraps around another

parts.note: to lour is to frown or scowl
an able seaman, a sailor, is abbreviated AB

explanation.surface: A grumpy seaman faces hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: The Twelve Labours of Hercules were his famous mighty feats.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules performed twelve heroic feats known by this name, so the plural means arduous tasks.

clue.text: See jazz group going round Asian capital

indicators.note: going round means one word encircles another

parts.note: a combo is a small jazz band
lo is an old word for see or behold

explanation.surface: Watch a band touring an Asian city.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is the commercial capital and largest city of Sri Lanka.

clue.text: Castle in the air?

explanation.walkthrough: A castle in the air is a daydream; read literally, it is the chess piece of the same name as a crow-like black bird, which flies.
explanation.definitionFit: The chess piece also called a castle shares its name with a gregarious crow.

clue.text: Criticism we hear for us fort

indicators.note: we hear says the word is spoken, its sound giving the spelling

parts.note: knocks are criticisms, as in taking knocks

explanation.surface: Rumoured criticism of a military base.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'us' as US: Fort Knox in Kentucky holds America's gold reserves.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kentucky army post holding the American gold reserve is named this way.

clue.text: Victoria thumbed by Jack for a lift?

definitions.text: thumbed by Jack for a lift?

explanation.surface: A woman named Victoria is hitchhiking with a man called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria is a variety of this fruit, and in the nursery rhyme Little Jack Horner 'put in his thumb and pulled out' one; 'lift' is the pulling out, not hitchhiking.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria is a popular variety of the fruit, and the nursery rhyme boy pulls one out of a pie with his thumb.

clue.text: Light joinery?

explanation.surface: A remark about carpentry that is not heavy work.
explanation.walkthrough: A link was a torch carried to light the way in old streets; a link also joins things.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a torch was called this, and a connecting piece or bond joins two things.

clue.text: The ultimate loser

explanation.surface: Someone is described as the biggest failure of all.
explanation.definitionFit: The final one is the ultimate, and whoever comes in at the back of a race is the loser.

clue.text: Chump has joint found by school principal

parts.note: a knuckle is a finger joint
the head is the headteacher in charge of a school

explanation.surface: A fool has a joint discovered by the headteacher.
explanation.walkthrough: Chump suggests a chop, which fits 'joint' as meat; here it means an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a stupid person.

clue.text: Met near exit when about to finish off

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: Someone met close to the way out just as they were about to kill.
explanation.definitionFit: To destroy completely or kill is to wipe out.
